title: Watchers and Nephilim as the exile-era unions
statement: The Watchers and the Nephilim are distinct: 'Watcher' designates the heavenly functionaries who, in the Enochic narrative, descend at Hermon, take human wives, and transmit forbidden arts, while 'Nephilim' names the mighty offspring of those unions in Genesis 6:4 — fathers and children of one antediluvian episode, collapsed together only by later reception; and the corpus identifies that episode with the exiled creators' unions with human women and the resulting offspring in the canon's account of the exile era.

includes: The textual-distinction layer, which is an inferred reading with strong scholarly support: Genesis 6:1-4 compresses what 1 Enoch makes explicit — the Watchers father, the giants are their children; the gigantes rendering, the uncertain 'fallen ones' gloss, and the West's loss of the Enochic narrative drove the later collapse of the two

The identification layer, which is framework: the episode read as the exiled creators' unions with human women and their mighty offspring (TBWTT ch. 2), placing it in the exile era of the conflict recorded as woh-claim-0008
The reception-history observation: the fusion of Watchers and Nephilim into one category is a datable development, not a feature of the earliest texts
excludes: Identity of Watchers with Nephilim, which the record exists to deny
One-to-one identification of named Watchers (Shemihazah, Asael) with named individuals in the canon's account
The forbidden-arts catalogue as literal technology inventory; what was transmitted is read at the level the sources state
Historicity of giants as a biological claim beyond what the canon's account of the offspring asserts
The Watchers' condemnation theology of 1 Enoch as canon; the Enochic moral frame and the canon's political frame are kept distinct

source_references.locator: Chapter 2: the exiled creators, their unions with human women, and the resulting mighty offspring of Genesis 6

The descent at Hermon, the oath, the wives, the transmitted arts, and the giant offspring (chs. 6-11)
The standard critical commentary on the Book of the Watchers
The reception history of the Watchers tradition and its loss in the West
The critical treatment of Genesis 6:1-4 as compressed narrative

alternatives.statement: Genesis 6:1-4 is a demoted mythological fragment retained to introduce the flood; it records theology, not an event, and 1 Enoch is exegetical expansion rather than independent memory.
The benei ha-elohim are the line of Seth, not heavenly beings — the traditional alternative that dissolves the episode entirely.
The Enochic Watchers narrative is Second Temple polemic against illegitimate priestly marriages or Hellenistic culture-heroes, explaining the forbidden-arts catalogue without any remembered unions.
The canon's exile-era unions and the Enochic descent are separate stories that the corpus maps onto each other; the identification is supplied by the framework, not by either text.

revision_triggers: Claim woh-claim-0001 or woh-claim-0008 is revised or retired.
Source-language review of the Genesis or Enoch renderings materially changes the fathers/children reading.
The identification fails against the canon's fuller context (the canon-mapping alternative vindicated).
Public prose begins identifying named Watchers with named canon figures or treating the arts catalogue as inventory, which this record excludes.
